title: Esther
subtitle: A queen in Persia, a decree of death, and the feast of Purim

lenses.name: History as told
lenses.desc: The traditional reading, Jewish and Christian: Esther is a true account of how the Jews of the Persian Empire were saved from Haman's plot under King Ahasuerus (usually identified with Xerxes I, 486–465 BC), and of how the feast of Purim began. The Talmud says the men of the Great Assembly wrote it down (Bava Batra 15a).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Many scholars read Esther as a court story or historical novella, set in a real Persian court but shaped by storytelling patterns such as reversal, banquets and the wise courtier, written to explain and authorize Purim. They debate its date (Persian or Hellenistic), its links to the Greek versions, and how much of it is history.

lenses.name: Persian records
lenses.desc: Esther is set at Susa, a Persian royal city that has been excavated. Greek writers such as Herodotus describe Xerxes' court, his queen Amestris, the royal post and the king's banquets, and Persian tablets from Persepolis and Babylonia name officials called Marduka, a form of the name Mordecai. How closely these sources fit the book is debated.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Esther is the Megillah, read aloud twice on Purim, and the Talmud tractate Megillah discusses it at length. The rabbis note that God's name never appears in the Hebrew text and find God hidden in the story (Chullin 139b links the name Esther to 'I will hide my face', Deuteronomy 31:18).

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Christians read Esther as a story of God's unseen care for his people and of courage at the right time (4:14). The Greek Esther, with six longer passages (Additions A–F) that add prayers and the name of God, is part of Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians; Protestants follow the shorter Hebrew. Some, such as Luther, were uneasy with the book.

lead: Esther is the story of how the Jews scattered through the Persian Empire were saved from destruction. King Ahasuerus throws a vast feast, deposes Queen Vashti when she refuses to come at his command, and chooses a new queen from the young women of his empire. The one he picks is Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, who has told her to keep her people a secret. When Mordecai will not bow to the king's favorite, Haman the Agagite, Haman casts lots to pick a day and wins a royal decree to wipe out every Jew in the empire.

Mordecai tells Esther that she may have come to the throne "for a time like this," and she risks her life by going to the king unasked. In a chain of banquets and reversals, Haman is hanged on the very pole he set up for Mordecai, Mordecai rises to Haman's place, and a second decree lets the Jews defend themselves. The book ends by setting up the feast of Purim, named for Haman's lots. In the Hebrew text God is never named, yet the story is full of timing that readers have always taken as God's hidden hand.
facts: Not named. The Talmud says the men of the Great Assembly wrote it down (Bavli Bava Batra 15a). Some medieval Jewish commentators, among them Ibn Ezra, and many Christian writers credited Mordecai, because he "wrote these things" (9:20). Most scholars see an unnamed Jewish writer of the eastern diaspora, using an older story and adding the Purim letters of chapter 9.

The story is set in the reign of Ahasuerus, almost certainly Xerxes I (486–465 BC), from his third year (1:3, about 483 BC) to his twelfth (3:7, about 474 BC) and after. Most scholars date the writing to the late Persian or early Greek period (about 400–200 BC); some argue for soon after the events, and a few older scholars for the Maccabean age. A note at the end of the Greek Esther (Addition F) dates its arrival in Egypt to "the fourth year of Ptolemy and Cleopatra," most likely 78–77 BC (some say 114 or 48 BC), so the book was known in Greek by then.

Susa, the Persian winter capital, in what is now southwest Iran, and the provinces of an empire that ran "from India to Cush" (1:1). Jews lived throughout it, scattered there since the Babylonian exile.

Narrative: a court story built on banquets, decrees and reversals, ending with letters that set up the feast of Purim (9:20–32). Many call it a historical novella; traditional readers read it as history.
Hebrew, of a late kind, with many Persian loanwords. The Greek versions add six passages (Additions A–F) not in the Hebrew.

10 chapters, 167 verses in the Hebrew. The Greek Esther (Septuagint) adds about 107 verses in six Additions. In Hebrew Bibles Esther is one of the Writings and one of the five Megillot (scrolls read at festivals), read at Purim; the Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) lists it between Daniel and Ezra, and printed Hebrew Bibles put it last of the five Megillot, after Ecclesiastes. Protestant Bibles place it after Nehemiah; Catholic and Orthodox Bibles after Tobit and Judith, with the Additions.

audience.to: Jews living as a minority among the nations, in the Persian Empire or the Greek kingdoms that followed it: families whose parents had been carried off from Judah and who now worked, traded and sometimes served at court in a foreign land, under kings who could be generous one day and deadly the next. Many of them had not gone back to Jerusalem with the returns told in Ezra and Nehemiah. The book's own frame is the feast of Purim, kept on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar by Jews scattered province by province and city by city (9:27–28).
audience.why: To tell them how their people had been saved in Persia, and to set the feast of Purim on that memory, so that every generation would keep it with feasting and gifts (9:20–32). It shows Jews far from the land and the Temple how to live faithfully at a foreign court: loyal to the king where they can be, unbending where loyalty to their people is at stake, and ready to risk everything for one another. It also answers a hard question: where is God when he seems silent? The book never names him, but its timing and reversals invite readers to see that the Jews of the diaspora are not forgotten. Knowing this audience explains why the story is set entirely outside the land, why the heroes are court officials rather than priests or prophets, and why the ending dwells on a feast that could be kept anywhere.
views: Traditional readers, Jewish and Christian, take it as a record of real events written down soon after them, perhaps from Persian court records (2:23; 10:2), to establish Purim.

Many scholars read it as a court tale or historical novella written in the eastern diaspora in the late Persian or early Greek period, to explain and authorize Purim and to encourage Jews living under foreign rule (Fox; Levenson; Berlin).
Some read it as composed above all to be read aloud at Purim, with its comedy, exaggeration and reversals suited to a carnival-like feast (Berlin).

The colophon of the Greek Esther (Addition F) says the 'letter of Purim' was brought to Egypt, probably in 78–77 BC. For those Greek-speaking Jews, the Additions and the colophon framed the book as a sacred, prayerful history with God openly at work. Some scholars also date the Hebrew book itself to the Hellenistic period, for Jews living under Greek kings.

authorship: Jewish tradition says the men of the Great Assembly, the council that the rabbis believed led the Jews after the return, wrote Esther down (Bavli Bava Batra 15a), and many readers took Mordecai's letters (9:20, 29) as the source of the account, so that Mordecai himself was its author or chief witness. On this view the book was written soon after the events, perhaps drawing on Persian court records (2:23; 10:2), to establish Purim. Its knowledge of Persian words, titles and customs, and the absence of Greek words, fit a writer of the Persian period.

Most scholars think an unnamed Jewish author of the eastern diaspora wrote the book in the late Persian or early Greek period, about 400–200 BC. They point to its late Hebrew, the narrator's distance from Ahasuerus ("This was the Ahasuerus who ...", 1:1), and storytelling features such as the reversals, the numbers and the irrevocable laws. Many, following Clines and Fox, think the book grew in stages: an earlier court story, perhaps close to the Hebrew original behind the Greek Alpha Text, was expanded with the Purim material of 9:20–32 and the closing notice of chapter 10. Older critics (Paton) dated it to the Maccabean age, about 165 BC; few hold that now.

The Septuagint and the Alpha Text add six passages (A–F), probably composed between about 200 and 78 BC, some in Greek (the royal letters B and E) and some perhaps in Hebrew or Aramaic. The colophon (Addition F) says a man named Lysimachus in Jerusalem translated the 'letter of Purim' and that it was brought to Egypt in the fourth year of Ptolemy and Cleopatra.

The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English Translation

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. Each verse was drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew, then checked against other English versions and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. Long Hebrew sentences, such as 1:1–8 and 8:9, are split. Key terms match the rest of the site: hesed is "loyal love"; Shushan habbirah is "the fortress at Susa," as in Nehemiah 1:1; dat is "law"; 'ets, the traditional "gallows," is "pole"; Haman's title tsorer hayyehudim is "the enemy of the Jews"; pur is "Pur, that is, the lot"; the courtly im 'al hammelekh tov is "If the king thinks it good," as in Nehemiah 2:5; and the three verbs of the decrees are "annihilate, kill and destroy" (3:13; 8:11).

The text and the Greek

The Plain English Translation follows the Leningrad Codex throughout. Hebrew and English verse numbers are the same in Esther. The Greek Esther comes in two forms, the Septuagint and the shorter Alpha Text, both with six long Additions (A–F). The Additions are not part of the Plain English Translation; where they fall, a variant summarizes them (before 1:1; after 3:13; after 4:17; at 5:1–2; after 8:12; after 10:3). Greek readings are cited from Rahlfs' edition of the Septuagint (the Old Greek) and from the Alpha Text as edited by Hanhart and translated by Karen Jobes in the New English Translation of the Septuagint (NETS), which prints the two Greek texts side by side.

Other translations

The Berean Standard Bible (2023), the King James Version (1611/1769), the American Standard Version (1901), Young's Literal Translation (1898) and the World English Bible can be shown for comparison. The KJV follows the Hebrew and prints the Additions, if at all, among the Apocrypha as "the rest of Esther."

sections.h: The God who is not named
sections.b:
The Hebrew Esther never names God. It mentions the king of Persia about 190 times and the God of Israel not once; no one prays, no one goes to the Temple, and the law of Moses is never cited. The only hints are Mordecai's words that rescue will come "from somewhere else" and "who knows?" (4:14), the fasting of 4:3 and 4:16, and the many reversals, which the book sums up in a phrase: "it was turned upside down" (9:1).

Readers have explained the silence in several ways. God hidden. The rabbis linked Esther's name to Deuteronomy 31:18, "On that day I will keep my face hidden" (Bavli Chullin 139b): the book shows God at work in a time when he hides his face, and its silence is its message. Most Jewish and Christian readers take this view, and it has made Esther the Bible's great book of providence. A festival scroll. Some suggest that a book to be read at a noisy feast, with drinking, avoided God's name so it would not be spoken lightly; others that it came from Persian court records that would not name a Jewish God. A secular story. Some critical scholars think the writer simply told a story of human courage and Jewish survival, and left theology to the reader. Medieval readers found the name YHWH hidden in acrostics at 1:20, 5:4, 5:13 and 7:7, and some manuscripts mark them; most scholars think that is chance. The Greek Esther, by contrast, names God more than fifty times, adds prayers and a God-sent dream, and says plainly that "God changed the spirit of the king" (Addition D).

sections.h: The Greek Esther and its Additions
sections.b:
There are two Greek forms of Esther. The Septuagint (the "B-text," printed by Rahlfs and Hanhart) is a free translation of a Hebrew text much like ours. The Alpha Text (also called the "A-text" or "L-text," once thought Lucianic) is shorter, differs in many details and ends differently; Clines, Fox and Jobes argue that it was translated from a different and possibly earlier Hebrew form of the story. Both contain six Additions not found in any Hebrew manuscript:

A, before 1:1: Mordecai's dream of two dragons and a little spring that becomes a river, and the eunuchs' plot. B, after 3:13: the text of the king's decree against the Jews. C, after 4:17: the prayers of Mordecai and Esther. D, in place of 5:1–2: Esther's approach to the king, her fainting and God's turning of the king's heart. E, after 8:12: the king's second decree, which calls Haman a Macedonian traitor and praises the Jews' laws. F, after 10:3: the interpretation of the dream and a note on the translation.

The Additions give God and prayer a central place, answer the moral questions the Hebrew leaves open (why Mordecai would not bow, how Esther could live as a gentile's wife), and make the story more like Daniel. Catholic and Orthodox Christians read the Greek Esther with the Additions as Scripture (deuterocanonical). Jerome, translating from the Hebrew for the Latin Vulgate (about AD 400), moved the Additions to the end of the book and marked them as not in the Hebrew, which is why older Bibles number them 10:4–16:24. Protestant Bibles follow the Hebrew and, if they print the Additions, put them among the Apocrypha. The Hebrew text is the base of this site; the variants give the Additions where they fall.

The case for history. The writer knows the Persian court well: Susa's palace and fortress, Persian words and titles, the seven nobles with access to the king, the royal post, the records of benefactors, the rules of access, the Persian taste for banquets. The dates fit Xerxes I, whose temper and harem Greek writers describe; tablets from Persepolis and Babylonia name an official called Marduka, perhaps Mordecai; and the book presents itself as history, pointing to "the book of the daily records" of the kings (10:2). Traditional Jewish and Christian readers, and some modern scholars such as Baldwin and Yamauchi, defend it as substantially historical.

The case for story. Herodotus names Xerxes' queen Amestris, not Vashti or Esther, and says Persian kings married only within seven noble families. A Persian law that cannot be revoked is unknown outside Esther and Daniel. The 127 provinces, the 180-day feast, the 10,000 talents, the eleven-month warning of a massacre and the 75,000 dead are on a scale many find unlikely, and the plot is built on symmetrical reversals and coincidences. Most critical scholars (Fox, Levenson, Berlin, Clines) read Esther as a historical novella or diaspora court tale: a story set in a real empire, written to explain Purim and to say something true about Jewish life among the nations, but not a chronicle.

Between the two. Many readers hold that the book may preserve a real memory of danger and deliverance in the Persian period, told in the shape of a story. Berlin suggests reading it as a festival comedy, with farce and exaggeration fitting the feast it founds. How a reader decides affects details but not the book's main claims: that Jews in exile faced deadly hatred, and that they were saved.

Achashverosh is the Hebrew form of the Persian name Xshayarsha, Greek Xerxes, and almost all scholars identify the king with Xerxes I (486–465 BC), son of Darius I. His empire reached "from India all the way to Cush" (1:1), as his own inscriptions say, and Ezra 4:6 puts an Ahasuerus between Darius and Artaxerxes, which fits. The book's dates then run from his third year (483 BC, 1:3) through Esther's coming to the king in his seventh (479/478 BC, 2:16), just after his defeat in Greece, to the lots of his twelfth (474 BC, 3:7) and the day of Adar the next spring.

The Septuagint and Josephus call the king Artaxerxes, and some ancient and older readers identified him with Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC), or even Artaxerxes II. The Alpha Text, like the Hebrew, calls him Ahasuerus (Assueros). Placing Esther under Xerxes sets it between the Temple's completion under Darius (Ezra 6:15, 515 BC) and the missions of Nehemiah (445 BC; Nehemiah 2) and, on the usual dating, Ezra (458 BC; Ezra 7) under Artaxerxes I, though some date Ezra to 398 BC under Artaxerxes II, so that the book shows the Jews who stayed in the east in the same generations as the returns to Judah.

Esther is the founding story of Purim, named for the lot (pur) that Haman cast (3:7; 9:24–26). It is kept on the fourteenth of Adar, and on the fifteenth in walled cities, as in Susa (9:17–19), about February or March. Its customs come from the book itself: the public reading of the scroll (the Megillah) in the evening and the morning, feasting and joy, sending portions of food to one another, and gifts to the poor (9:19, 22). The Fast of Esther is kept on 13 Adar (4:16; 9:31). In the synagogue the reader often reads the names of Haman's ten sons in one breath (9:7–10), and the congregation makes noise to drown out Haman's name. The Sabbath before Purim is "Remember" (Zakhor), with the reading of Deuteronomy 25:17–19 on Amalek.

Purim is the only biblical feast not commanded in the law of Moses. It was set up by Mordecai's and Esther's letters and the Jews' own acceptance (9:20–32), and it can be kept anywhere, by Jews living among the nations. 2 Maccabees 15:36 calls it "Mordecai's day," and Josephus describes it (Antiquities 11.292–295). Some scholars have looked for its origin in a Babylonian or Persian festival, which the Jews of the east adapted; others think the book's story is its real origin. Either way, the scroll and the feast have been bound together for over two thousand years.

sections.h: Was Esther Scripture? Qumran and the rabbis
sections.b:
Esther is the only book of the Hebrew Bible of which no copy has been identified among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and Purim is absent from the Qumran calendars. Some think this is chance; others that the community rejected the book, perhaps because of its marriage to a gentile, its silence about God, or a feast not in the law. A few Aramaic fragments that some scholars once called "Proto-Esther" (4Q550) tell a court story with Persian names, but most now doubt any direct link.

The early rabbis debated it too. The Talmud records that the sage Samuel said Esther "does not make the hands impure," the rabbis' way of saying a scroll is not holy Scripture to be handled with special care. The Gemara explains that Samuel held it was inspired to be read aloud but not to be written as Scripture; other sages, among them Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Akiva, argued that it was inspired outright (Bavli Megillah 7a). The same passage tells how Esther asked the sages to fix her book and feast for all generations, and they worried that doing so would provoke the nations. In the end the rabbis accepted it fully, and the Jerusalem Talmud says that when the Prophets and Writings pass away, the Torah and the scroll of Esther will remain (Yerushalmi Megillah 1:5).

Among Christians, Melito of Sardis (about AD 170) left Esther off his list of Old Testament books, Athanasius counted it among books to be read but outside the canon, and Luther said he was so hostile to it that he wished it did not exist (Table Talk). Most churches nonetheless received it, and the Greek form became Scripture in the East and, through the Vulgate, in the West.

On the day set for their destruction, the Jews, armed by the second decree (8:11), kill their attackers: five hundred in the fortress at Susa and Haman's ten sons, three hundred more in Susa on a second day that Esther requests, and seventy-five thousand in the provinces (9:5–16). They take no plunder. Readers have answered this in very different ways.

Self-defense. Many Jewish and Christian readers stress that the first decree was still law: the Jews' enemies had leave to kill them, and the second decree let the Jews "stand up for their lives" (8:11; 9:16) against "those who hated them" and attacked. The text three times says they did not touch the plunder (9:10, 15, 16), which the decree allowed, as if to show they fought to survive, not to profit, and to set them apart from Saul, who took the spoil of Amalek (1 Samuel 15:9).

Troubling revenge. Other readers find the scene disturbing: the scale of the killing, the request for a second day, the hanging of the ten sons' bodies, and the phrase "however they wanted" (9:5). Some Christian commentators, Luther among them, judged the book harshly for this, and some critical scholars, such as Paton, wrote of its spirit of revenge in terms now seen as colored by prejudice against Jews. Many modern Jewish and Christian readers wrestle honestly with the chapter and reject any use of it to justify violence. On Purim 1994 a Jewish extremist, Baruch Goldstein, killed 29 Muslim worshipers at the Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron; many linked the date to the themes of Purim and Amalek. Israel's government, its chief rabbis and Jewish leaders around the world condemned the attack, though a small fringe honored him.

Story and feast. Scholars who read Esther as a carnival story (Berlin) or a tale of reversal (Fox) note that the numbers belong to the exaggeration of the whole book, that the chapter mirrors the decree of chapter 3 point by point, and that the feast it founds celebrates rest from enemies, not their deaths (9:17–22). The chapter page for chapter 9 gives the details.

In the Hebrew Bible, Esther is one of the Writings (Ketuvim) and one of the five Megillot, the scrolls read at festivals: Song of Songs (Passover), Ruth (Weeks), Lamentations (the Ninth of Av), Ecclesiastes (Booths) and Esther (Purim). The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) lists it between Daniel and Ezra; the Leningrad Codex places it after Lamentations and before Daniel; most printed Hebrew Bibles put it last of the five Megillot, and the Writings then go on to Daniel, Ezra–Nehemiah and Chronicles. Christian Bibles place it among the histories, after Nehemiah (Protestant) or after Tobit and Judith (Catholic and Orthodox), so that it closes the story of the Persian period begun in Ezra.

Esther speaks to the rest of the Bible in many ways. It retells the Joseph story at a Persian court, it takes up the feud with Amalek from Exodus 17, Deuteronomy 25 and 1 Samuel 15, and it stands beside Daniel as a book about Jews serving foreign kings. The New Testament never quotes it. Josephus retells it with the Greek Additions (Antiquities 11.184–296), the two Aramaic Targums (Targum Rishon and the longer Targum Sheni) expand it with legends, and the Midrash Esther Rabbah and the Talmud's tractate Megillah comment on it verse by verse.

spec.title: Claude's theory: two hidden identities
spec.body: My own reading: the book hides two identities and reveals them together. Esther hides that she is a Jew (2:10, 20), and the book hides the God of the Jews. Each stays out of sight while the danger grows. When Esther finally says "my people" to the king (7:3–4), the story turns, and from that moment the reversals pile up so fast that readers find it hard not to name the one behind them. The Talmud already ties Esther's name to God's hidden face (Bavli Chullin 139b), and many scholars note that Esther's concealment parallels the book's reticence about God (Fox and Berlin among them). Reading the revelation of Esther's people in chapter 7 as the book's way of letting readers glimpse the hidden God is my own suggestion; it rests on the way 4:14 links Esther's coming forward to rescue "from somewhere else."

traditions.q: Is Esther Scripture, and do the Greek Additions belong to it?
views: Yes, with the Additions. The Council of Trent received the books of the Old Testament with all their parts as they stood in the Latin Bible, so the Additions to Esther are Scripture (deuterocanonical). Modern Catholic Bibles print them where they fall in the story, lettered A–F.

Yes, with the Additions. The Orthodox read Esther in the Greek form of the Septuagint, which has always included Mordecai's dream and the prayers of Mordecai and Esther, so in their Bible God is named throughout the book.

The Hebrew Esther is Scripture and the Additions are Apocrypha. Luther himself was uneasy with the book: he wrote that it deserved to be left out of the canon more than any other (The Bondage of the Will, 1525), and said he wished it and 2 Maccabees did not exist, because they Judaize too much (Table Talk). Lutheran churches kept it in their Bibles all the same.
Article 6 counts Esther among the canonical books, and lists "the rest of the Book of Esther" among the books read for example of life but not to establish any doctrine.

The Hebrew Esther is Scripture (Westminster Confession 1.2), and the Additions are Apocrypha with no authority in the church (1.3). Reformed preachers have often prized the Hebrew book, with its silence about God, as the Bible's great lesson in providence.
